briefs.headline: Man sells house, skips ITR and then claims capital gains exemption; why ITAT gave relief
briefs.deck: The Income Tax Department had information that the man purchased an immovable property valued at Rs 45 lakh during the relevant year. Since he had not filed his income tax return, proceedings were initiated under Section 147 of the Income Tax Act. A notice under Section 148 was issued on March 24, 2024.
briefs.bodyText:
Can you claim an exemption in your income tax return if you have not filed it originally and only initiate ITR filing after getting a notice from the 
Income Tax Department
?
In a relief for taxpayers, the Mumbai bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) has ruled that an exemption claim under Section 54 of the Income Tax (I-T) Act for reinvestment of capital gains in a new house cannot be rejected merely because the taxpayer did not initially file an income tax return.
The tribunal held that such a claim can be considered and allowed when it is made during reassessment proceedings.
What the case is about
The case concerned an individual taxpayer who had not submitted an original income tax return under Section 139(1).
The dispute concerned the assessment year 2017-18. According to the tribunal's order, the Income Tax Department had information that the man purchased an immovable property valued at Rs 45 lakh during the relevant year. Since he had not filed his income tax return, proceedings were initiated under Section 147 of the Income Tax Act. A notice under Section 148 was issued on March 24, 2024.
The man filed his return in response to the notice on April 4, 2024. In it, he claimed an exemption under Section 54 on the capital gains from the sale of a residential property. The sale agreement was dated.
In his ITR, the man reported long-term capital gains from the sale of a residential property and sought an exemption of Rs 49 lakh under Section 54, citing his investment in another residential property.
Section 54 of the Act allows individuals to claim an exemption on long-term capital gains arising from the sale of a residential property to the extent that the gains are reinvested in purchasing another residential house within the stipulated period.
The assessing officer turned down the assessee’s claim, citing the absence of an original income tax return.
The assessment order referred to Section 54D while disallowing the claim made under Section 54, and added Rs 31,38,256 to his income.
The man challenged the addition before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), but the appellate authority upheld the decision. It relied on the Supreme Court's judgment in 
CIT vs Sun Engineering Works (P.) Ltd.
, which addresses the limits on claims that can be raised during reassessment proceedings.
Why ITAT Mumbai ruled in assessee’s favour
ITAT Mumbai clarified that although reassessment proceedings cannot be used to reopen matters unrelated to income that has escaped assessment, taxpayers can raise claims that have a direct connection with such income.
The ITAT observed that the capital gains in this case were themselves the income that had escaped assessment, making the claim for exemption under Section 54 directly relevant to the calculation of that income.
The order explains that the escaped income in this case was the long-term capital gain from the sale of a residential property. The Section 54 claim related to the computation of that very income and was not an unrelated claim raised during reassessment.
It therefore held that the exemption request could not be classified as a new or unrelated claim that was impermissible during reassessment proceedings.
The tribunal also cited earlier judicial rulings which established that Section 54 does not make filing an income tax return by the prescribed due date a mandatory condition for claiming the exemption. It stressed that a claim submitted in a return filed in response to a reassessment notice cannot be turned down simply because it was made late or the taxpayer had not filed an original return.
The order also records that, in a case involving the man’s wife, the assessing officer had accepted a Section 54 deduction claimed in a return filed in response to a reassessment notice for the remaining 50% share of the investment in the new property. The tribunal noted this circumstance while considering the man’s argument.
In its reasoning, the tribunal stated that the earlier decisions supported allowing the claim to be examined rather than rejecting it solely because no original return had been filed. It concluded: “We thus, respectfully relying on the above judgments are inclined to allow the appeal of the Assessee, therefore, remand the case to the file of the AO for decision afresh on the claim of the Assessee under section 54 of the Act within the parameters and/or conditions set out in section 54 of the Act but not otherwise.”
The ITAT consequently overturned the orders passed by the lower authorities and sent the case back to the assessing officer for fresh consideration.
It directed the officer to assess the taxpayer’s entitlement to the Section 54 exemption on merits and grant the benefit if the applicable statutory requirements are met.

briefs.headline: He worked for less than 5 years, denied gratuity; why court ordered payout with 10% interest
briefs.deck: The man joined the Bengaluru Metro Rail Corporation (BMRCL) as an assistant engineer on July 6, 2017. He resigned on March 19, 2022, and was formally relieved of his duties on April 18, 2022. His total period of employment amounted to four years, nine months and 12 days. After leaving the corporation, he made several representations seeking payment of gratuity. He claimed Rs 1.85 lakh…
briefs.bodyText:
Are you entitled to a gratuity payout if you have not completed five years of continuous service with your employer? While the Labour codes have undergone a change and some rules have changed, certain pending cases also raise this important question.
In one such case, the Karnataka High Court has ruled that an employee who leaves a job before completing five years of continuous service can still qualify for gratuity if the conditions laid down under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972
, are met.
The court held that where an employee has worked for at least 240 days during the 12 calendar months immediately preceding his resignation, the period can be treated as a complete year of service for determining gratuity eligibility.
What the case is about
The dispute involved a former assistant engineer at 
Bangalore Metro
, whose claim for Rs 1.75 lakh in gratuity was rejected because his tenure fell short of five years.
He had worked for four years, nine months and 12 days.
The man joined the Bengaluru Metro Rail Corporation (BMRCL) as an assistant engineer on July 6, 2017. He resigned on March 19, 2022, and was formally relieved of his duties on April 18, 2022. His total period of employment amounted to four years, nine months and 12 days.
After leaving the corporation, he made several representations seeking payment of gratuity. He claimed Rs 1.85 lakh, calculating the amount on the basis of his last-drawn monthly salary of Rs 64,210.
BMRCL declined to release the payment, prompting him to approach the court.
Why the court ruled in favour of ex-employee
The Karnataka High Court observed that the dispute could not be decided simply by checking whether the man had completed five calendar years from the date he joined BMRCL.
His entitlement to gratuity had to be assessed by reading Section 4(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act alongside the definition of “continuous service” provided under Sections 2(c) and 2A.
The bench also made it clear that gratuity is not a discretionary payment or a benefit granted by an employer as a matter of goodwill, an ET report said. It is a statutory entitlement that becomes payable when the employee fulfils the conditions prescribed under the law.
Section 4(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act lays down the requirement of five years of continuous service, subject to certain specified exceptions.
However, the court said this provision cannot be considered on its own, without taking into account Section 2(c), which defines “continuous service” with reference to Section 2A.
Section 2A, in turn, sets out the statutory criteria for determining whether an employee has completed continuous service. Under the circumstances specified in sub-section (2), an employee can be deemed to have completed the prescribed period of continuous service if he has worked for at least 240 days during the relevant 12-calendar-month period.
The Karnataka High Court observed that the deeming provision is an integral part of the legal framework for determining continuous service, rather than a factor that can be disregarded.
Consequently, an employee’s eligibility cannot be decided merely by counting the calendar time between the date of joining and the end of employment. The actual number of days worked and the applicability of Section 2A of the Payment of Gratuity Act must also be examined.
Against this backdrop, the court identified the central issue in the man’s case as whether his employment during the fifth year met the statutory conditions and whether he could claim the benefit of the deeming provision on the basis of the facts placed before the statutory authorities.
The Karnataka High Court ruled in favour of the engineer and directed Bangalore Metro to pay him Rs 1.75 lakh along with interest at 10% from May 18, 2022.
Explaining the significance of the decision, Mayank Parashar, Legal Associate at Clasis Law-India, told ET: "Karnataka High Court has now re-settled the principle in the context of eligibility of the continuous service requirement for gratuity and concluded that employers should consider the definition of continuous service and key conditions for gratuity together. That’s said every employee who has completed 240 days in 6 days working and 190 days in 5 days working but has not completed the entire year should be considered eligible for gratuity."

briefs.headline: Western states drive car sales in Q2, Maharashtra leads
briefs.bodyText:
New Delhi: Maharashtra remained India's largest passenger vehicle market in July-Sept. Sales in the state rose about 25% from a year earlier to 1.6 lakh units, while national sales grew 30.7% to 13.6 lakh units, according to the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (Siam). Maharashtra's share of national sales fell from 12.7% to 12.1%.
The western region, which includes Maharashtra and Gujarat, retained its lead among Siam's four zones. It sold close to 4.3 lakh passenger vehicles in the second quarter of FY27, up about 25% from year earlier. With sales growing slower than the national market, the region's share slipped from about 33% to 32%.
Uttar Pradesh and Gujarat held on to second and third place, accounting for 9.8% and 8.3% of passenger vehicle sales, respectively.
Meanwhile, two-wheeler sales rose 15.2% year on year to 64.3 lakh units, the highest for any second quarter. The western region led this segment too, with sales rising about 9% to 21.1 lakh units a year earlier.
UP remained the largest two-wheeler market, with sales rising about 14% to close to 7.9 lakh units. Maharashtra held on to second place.

briefs.headline: Nvidia sets record with $65bn Q3 profit
briefs.bodyText:
Nvidia Corp sought to deliver a clear message during its first earnings update since the departure of long-time leader Jensen Huang: He's not coming back, and the company will be fine without him.
Total sales rose 103% to $115.8 billion for the third quarter of fiscal 2027. The champion of semiconductors for artificial intelligence once again exceeded expectations, both in terms of revenue and net income, which reached $65.3 billion.
The chip giant boosted its sales forecast for next year and vowed to improve Nvidia's access to critical supplies, while tamping down speculation that Huang might return. The company also added $150 billion to its stock-buyback programme.
The shares rose as much as 2.7% to $159.7 on Wednesday after trading got underway in New York. Nvidia's stock has tumbled in recent weeks, battered by the scandal and broader fears that AI spending is poised to slow. It's down about 17% this year.
"Our supply is growing, our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed," interim CEO Colette Kress said during a conference call with analysts Tuesday. 
"We've got this." It was a high-stakes moment for Kress, who took the reins last week after Huang's ouster - a chaotic exit spurred by multiple extramarital affairs and concerns that he was targeted by a Chinese espionage plot.
Nvidia has been the largest beneficiary of the AI build-out, and Huang served as the industry's biggest cheerleader. Now the company looks to ensure that its momentum won't be undermined by the controversy swirling around it.
"The cards of doubt seemed stacked so high. However, from a bird's-eye view it was a solid 3Q27 print," said Daniel Morgan, a senior portfolio manager at Synovus Trust. "The number of concerns surrounding Nvidia shares will most likely keep the shares range-bound." Bloomberg

briefs.headline: Megha Engg MD raises $700mn, to buy out founder uncle's stake
briefs.bodyText:
Hyderabad: One of India's biggest infrastructure companies is all set to see a change in its ownership pattern. Megha Engineering and Infrastructures Limited (MEIL) Group's MD, PV Krishna Reddy, has raised about $700 million (Rs 6,600 crore) from a consortium of global investors to buy out the 43% stake held by his uncle and MEIL group founder, P Pitchi Reddy.
The transaction, backed by investors including Davidson Kempner, Hillhouse Capital and Varde Partners, has been structured through a mix of structured equity and the proposed monetisation of select road assets. The Hyderabad-based conglomerate, however, refused to give details of the deal.
According to sources, the deadline for Krishna Reddy to acquire his uncle's stake as part of the family settlement arrangement was 2027. While earlier Pitchi Reddy held a 51% stake and Krishna Reddy held a 49% stake, Krishna Reddy had increased his stake to 57% over a period of time.
Sources said the deal values MEIL at about Rs 1 lakh crore, while its energy transition platform, EPTL, has been valued at around Rs 14,000 crore.
A farmer's son from Andhra Pradesh, Pitchi Reddy had started the company in 1989 as a small fabrication and pipe manufacturing workshop in Hyderabad's bustling Balanagar Industrial Estate. Its initial capital was just Rs 5 lakh. Krishna Reddy had joined the operation a couple of years later and played a key role in turning the workshop into an infrastructure giant over the past four decades. MEIL now has operations in more than 20 countries.
The group's businesses span irrigation, transport, hydrocarbons, power, manufacturing and clean mobility.

briefs.headline: 'India's challenge next year may be rupee's strength, not weakness': CEA Nageswaran
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The country's challenge next year may be managing the rupee's strength rather than its weakness, chief economic advisor (CEA) V Anantha Nageswaran said on Wednesday, amid ongoing geopolitical uncertainties. His remarks come against the backdrop of volatility in the domestic currency, which has been appreciating in recent weeks.
The rupee hit the lowest closing level of 96.88 against the US dollar on Oct 8, and since then it has rebounded, closing at 93.41 on Wednesday.
Speaking at an event organised by Ficci, Nageswaran said India's exports have reached $568 billion in the first seven months of this fiscal, and are likely to touch the $1 trillion mark by March 2027.
"...look at the export numbers this year (fiscal) in the first seven months, $568 billion. Those of us who are not that mathematically challenged, we can easily extrapolate this to a 12-month number and say that we will be close to achieving a ($) trillion," Nageswaran said.
India's total exports during April-Oct 2026-27 are estimated at $568.8 billion, up 16.7%. Total imports are estimated at $662.2 billion, a 16% rise year-on-year.
Nageswaran further said, "We are approaching the end of the calendar year in a far better frame of mind than we would have found ourselves in six months ago". And if the prognosis of oil prices and what happens to the AI valuations is any indication, then 2027-28 could also turn out to be a fairly good year in terms of growth and capital flows to India."

briefs.headline: Sebi studying various SLBM models: Pandey
briefs.deck: Sebi chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey revealed that the regulator is exploring international models for stock lending and borrowing. Speaking at the World Federation of Exchanges, he also dismissed the possibility of extending trading hours, citing heightened risks.
briefs.bodyText:
Mumbai: Sebi chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey on Wednesday said that the markets regulator was studying various models for stock lending-borrowing mechanism (SLBM) from around the world to have a suitable system for the Indian market. He also ruled out extending trading hours, saying such a change would mean increased risks, liquidity issues etc. The Sebi chief said there was no decision taken by the regulator relating to margin trade finance (MTF) rules.
Pandey was responding to reporters after addressing the 65th general assembly and annual meeting of the World Federation of Exchanges (WFE).
During his address, Pandey also said that technology will continue to reshape market infrastructure. "Artificial intelligence and advanced analytics offer significant opportunities in market surveillance, risk monitoring, regulatory compliance and investor services. At the same time, AI introduces challenges relating to model reliability, data governance, cybersecurity and dependence on a limited number of technology providers. Hence, the objective should be to encourage innovation while ensuring that governance and safeguards keep pace," he said.
The top regulator also said that many of the challenges that regulators around the world are facing currently are not confined to national boundaries. "Cyber threats, technological dependencies, market volatility and cross-border financial linkages affect exchanges and clearing corporations across jurisdictions. While our markets differ in size, structure and maturity, our underlying objectives remain similar: Fair and transparent markets, investor confidence and financial stability.
"
Pandey said that these are the areas where organisations such as WFE play a valuable role. On the issue of extending trading hours in India, Pandey said it's not a priority for the regulator because that could increase cybersecurity risks, overnight volatility and also bring with it liquidity concerns.
On the issue of SLBM, the Sebi chairman said that the regulator was in favour of transparent, exchange-based models for stock lending-borrowing mechanism.

stories.headline: Carlsen's forfeits spark domino effect! Two more GMs skip games at Total Chess Pilot
stories.deck: The recent decision by World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen to forfeit his Fast Classic games has sparked a debate on tournament rules and fair play. In light of this, fellow competitors Abhimanyu Mishra and Richard Rapport opted out of their final matches. Mishra mentioned fatigue and concerns about impact on his ratings, while Rapport skipped his concluding game following a previous loss.
stories.bodyText:
World No. 1 
Magnus Carlsen
's decision to forfeit his Fast Classic games after securing unassailable leads has triggered a domino effect at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot, with two more Grandmasters choosing to skip their matches on Wednesday.
India's R Vaishali and Armenia's Haik Martirosyan were left waiting in the playing hall after their respective opponents, Abhimanyu Mishra and Richard Rapport, decided not to turn up for the concluding Fast Classic games. The developments came after Carlsen had courted controversy by walking away from his matches against Kazakhstan's Bibisara Assaubayeva on consecutive days.
While Carlsen's actions had already raised questions about sportsmanship and the tournament's regulations, the decisions by Mishra and Rapport have added another layer to the debate over the format.
Mishra explains decision after Vaishali is handed eight points
Competing for places 21st to 24th, 17-year-old Mishra entered the final game with an 11-1 lead over Vaishali after winning the opening day's fixture 13-7. He had also secured the second day's match before the Fast Classic encounter, having built an advantage through the blitz and rapid games.
Mishra chose not to play the concluding contest, handing Vaishali all eight points on offer. However, his 11-9 victory in the day's overall score meant he won the tie and advanced.
"There's nothing to say," Vaishali said as she walked away from the playing area.
She will now face Uzbekistan's Nodirbek Abdusattorov in a match to avoid finishing last in the tournament.
Mishra later took to X to explain his decision, citing fatigue after an exhausting schedule and uncertainty over whether the remaining games in already-decided matches would count towards players' ratings.
"There's nothing to say" was Vaishali's brief reaction, while Mishra said he had approached the chief arbiter well in advance to seek permission not to play.
"Well in advance of the next game, I approached the chief arbiter to ask whether it would be acceptable for me not to show up. She told me that the decision was entirely mine and that it was perfectly acceptable not to play," he wrote.
He added that the demanding schedule, coupled with uncertainty surrounding the rating implications of the remaining games, had influenced his decision.
"Given that uncertainty, combined with the fatigue I felt, plus permission from the chief arbiter, I had sufficient reasons not to show up," Mishra said.
Rapport also skips game after losing tie
Rapport's decision came in a different context. The Hungarian Grandmaster had already lost his tie against Martirosyan and was trailing 2-10 on the second day after conceding the opening day's fixture 9-11.
He subsequently forfeited the Fast Classic game, leaving Martirosyan without an opponent for the concluding encounter.
The two walkovers followed Carlsen's repeated decision to skip the final game against Assaubayeva after taking commanding leads in their two-day tie.
Carlsen's actions put tournament format under scrutiny
Carlsen had already secured an 11-point advantage on the opening day against Assaubayeva after winning three of the four blitz games and two rapid games. He then forfeited the Fast Classic encounter, handing his opponent all eight points on offer, but still won the day's fixture 11.5-8.5.
The Norwegian repeated the move on Wednesday after building a 10-2 lead through the blitz and rapid games. Assaubayeva was again awarded the eight points, leaving the day's score tied 10-10. Carlsen, however, advanced on the strength of his opening-day victory.
Explaining his decision, Carlsen said the concluding game had little significance once the match was decided.
"There will be no classical game as I understood, the match is over. The only consequence of not showing up is that you will lose a totally meaningless game," he was quoted as saying by Norwegian broadcaster TV2.
Carlsen also admitted that he was not keen on playing more classical chess in the classification fixture.
"This is an awkward situation to be in, I would rather not play that much more classical anymore," he had said on Tuesday.
The Norwegian's decision attracted criticism, with American Grandmaster Hans Niemann alleging preferential treatment and insisting that the rules should be applied equally to all players. FIDE Chief Executive Adviser Emil Sutovsky described the conduct as unsportsmanlike, while India's Olympiad captain Srinath Narayanan also criticised the lack of courtesy.
Organisers looking at feedback ahead of 2027 edition
The controversy has also put the spotlight on the tournament's regulations, particularly the significance of Fast Classic games after a player has already secured qualification.
Total Chess CEO Kjell Madland said the Budapest pilot was intended to help organisers assess the format and identify possible refinements before the inaugural edition in March 2027.
"The Budapest pilot is an important learning exercise for Total Chess. While we have developed the format and regulations with considerable thought and input, the real test is how they work in a live competitive environment," Madland said in a statement.
He added that organisers wanted feedback directly from players and arbiters before deciding whether changes were necessary.
The organisers had not immediately confirmed whether Carlsen's forfeits would attract an automatic fine. With Mishra and Rapport now also having skipped their concluding games, the issue has become more pressing: whether the format needs clearer rules to ensure that every scheduled game is treated consistently, irrespective of whether a match has already been decided.

stories.headline: Dhoni and CSK: a match made in heaven
stories.deck: It was a bond that was established very quickly, grew with time and became an unshakeable relationship of near-equals though no one was in any doubt who was the dominant force driving it
stories.bodyText:
At first glance, it seemed like an unlikely match, but what a match it has turned out to be! Chennai Super Kings and Mahendra Singh Dhoni are comprehensively intertwined, inseparable and inextricable, one segueing seamlessly into the other, an incongruity in a world where ulterior motives and individual needs are usually the driving forces that define any relationship of convenience.
This has been anything but a relationship of convenience, of course. Dhoni gave the franchise everything he had without expecting much in return; the franchise gave the leader everything it could, also without expecting the moon. The offshoot of all this is that the rustic hero from Ranchi stormed the collective consciousness of the average conservative Chennaiite, charming a wide spectrum of the populace with his down-to-earth nature, his humility and modesty, his understated presence and his almost desperate desire to shun the limelight despite being the most public of personalities, all of which are almost second nature to those that make up the southern state.
Dhoni was three and a quarter years young in international cricket when he was snapped up by CSK at the inaugural IPL auction in 2008. Like Deccan Chargers (after V.V.S. Laxman turned down the offer so that the franchise could use that money to invest in Hyderabad cricket) and Rajasthan Royals, CSK was one of the three original franchises that didn’t have an icon player. Mumbai Indians boasted Sachin Tendulkar, Royal Challengers Bangalore had Rahul Dravid, Kolkata Knight Riders enjoyed the services of Sourav Ganguly, Delhi Daredevils had Virender Sehwag and Yuvraj Singh donned that role for Kings XI Punjab.

stories.headline: IND vs NZ, 1st Test: Nicholls, Phillips spark New Zealand fightback after Bumrah exploits
stories.deck: After Bumrah fiery spell and with the ball getting older and the pitch settling down, the Kiwi batters seldom appeared in discomfort
stories.bodyText:
Jasprit Bumrah continued his dream start with an early wicket in the second session, but Henry Nicholls and Glenn Phillips’ sensible batting sparked a New Zealand fightback after lunch. Riding on the duo’s unbeaten 79-run association for the sixth wicket, the home team reached 149 for five at tea on Day One of the first Test at the Basin Reserve on Thursday (November 19, 2026).
Nicholls, the standout batter of the day so far, continued his vigil from the first session and pounced on a freebie from Anshul Kamboj off the first ball after lunch. Kamboj strayed down the leg side and Nicholls tapped it to fine-leg for four. While the left-hander looked increasingly comfortable with every passing over, Tom Blundell was visibly struggling to negotiate Bumrah running in at full steam from the other end.
Bumrah had his man in the third over of the session, with Blundell hanging his bat out and captain Shubman Gill pouching a neat catch at first slip.
In came Phillips, who opened his account with a crisp cover drive off Bumrah. Had a controversial DRS review gone India’s way, the hosts could have been in deeper trouble. The ball appeared to have made three impacts — front pad, inside edge and back pad — but the TV umpire ruled it bat-first, leaving Gill animated in his discussion with the on-field umpire.
Thereafter, with Bumrah ending a marathon seven-over spell that included five after the break, the ball getting older and the pitch settling down, the Kiwi batters seldom appeared in discomfort. Nicholls brought up his maiden fifty against India in his seventh innings, pulling Kamboj for his seventh four, while Phillips made the most of the fuller deliveries bowled by Prasidh Krishna.
Washington Sundar, preferred ahead of Ravindra Jadeja, was introduced in the 42nd over, but Nicholls and Phillips continued to score freely. New Zealand added 89 runs for the loss of just one wicket in 26 overs in the session, wresting back some control after India’s early burst.

stories.headline: 'Thanks football': World Cup, Champions League winner Juan Mata retires at 38
stories.deck: Juan Mata, the former midfielder for Spain and Manchester United, has officially retired from professional football at the age of 38. His illustrious career was marked by triumphs, including a World Cup win and a Champions League title. In his final season with Melbourne Victory in the A-League, he was named the league's best player.
stories.bodyText:
Former Spain, Chelsea and 
Manchester United
 midfielder Juan Mata announced his retirement from professional football at the age of 38 on Wednesday, bringing the curtain down on a distinguished career that featured some of the biggest honours in the game.
The Spaniard, who won the FIFA World Cup, the UEFA European Championship and the 
UEFA Champions League
, confirmed his decision through a video posted on social media, recorded in the dressing room at Juventud Estadio in Oviedo, where he began playing organised football at the age of 10.
"Sometimes, to love is to let go... Thanks football," Mata wrote in his post.
His retirement comes after a successful final stint in Australia's A-League with Melbourne Victory, where he enjoyed an impressive 2025-26 campaign. He scored five goals and provided 13 assists, earning the Johnny Warren Medal as the league's best player. He also won the best playmaker award.
From Spain's golden generation to European glory
Mata was part of Spain's golden generation that dominated international football between 2008 and 2012. He was a member of the squad that won the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, where Spain defeated the Netherlands 1-0 after extra time.
Two years later, he scored in Spain's 4-0 victory over Italy in the Euro 2012 final, helping the country retain its continental crown. 
He finished his international career with 41 appearances and 10 goals.
At club level, Mata began his journey in Real Madrid's youth academy before making his breakthrough at Valencia, where he won the Copa del Rey in 2008.
His move to Chelsea in 2011 marked another defining chapter. In his first season at Stamford Bridge, he helped the London club win the Champions League in 2012, defeating Bayern Munich in the final. He also lifted the FA Cup in 2012 and the Europa League in 2013.
Mata joined Manchester United in January 2014 and spent around eight-and-a-half years at Old Trafford, making 285 appearances. His honours included the FA Cup in 2016, the Europa League in 2017, the League Cup and the Community Shield.
Trophy-winning journey continued after England
After leaving England in 2022, Mata continued adding silverware to his collection. He won the Turkish league title with Galatasaray in the 2022-23 season before helping Japan's Vissel Kobe secure the J.League crown in 2023.
He subsequently moved to Australia, playing for Melbourne Victory and Western Sydney Wanderers. Following his departure from Victory in September, he committed to an ownership interest in the club and took on the role of chair of its football committee.
Beyond his achievements on the pitch, Mata also co-founded Common Goal in 2017, an initiative encouraging footballers to pledge one per cent of their income towards community projects and social change.
With his retirement, one of the most decorated midfielders of Spain's golden era brings an end to a career spanning nearly two decades and multiple continents.

briefs.headline: DRS drama! Shubman Gill has words with umpire: 'Height hai, bat nahi hai'
briefs.deck: Shubman Gill won the toss and elected to bowl against New Zealand. Mohammed Siraj and Ravindra Jadeja were left out of the playing XI as India opted for a four-pronged pace attack. Gill went with four pacers - Jasprit Bumrah, Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj and Prasidh Krishna. Washington Sundar was included as the spin-bowling all-rounder.
briefs.bodyText:
India captain 
Shubman Gill
 was visibly unhappy after India lost a review against 
Glenn Phillips
 on the opening day of the first Test against New Zealand at the Basin Reserve in Wellington.
The incident took place in the 31st over of New Zealand's innings when JJasprit Bumrah bowled a delivery that moved back towards Glenn Phillips and beat his bat. India appealed for LBW, but the on-field umpire turned it down.
Gill discussed the decision with Bumrah before taking the review.
Bumrah felt the ball was too high and told his captain, 
"height hai"
 [it's high].
Gill, however, felt Phillips had not edged the ball and said, "
bat nahi hai"
 [no bat].
The Snickometer showed a big spike when the ball passed close to the bat. However, the front-on replay did not clearly show an inside edge.
Third umpire Paul Reiffel asked for another replay in slow motion. He felt there was a slight deflection and upheld the on-field umpire Richard Illingworth's not-out decision.
Gill was unhappy with the decision. He told Illingworth that there was a gap between the bat and ball and that the delivery had hit Phillips' back pad first.
Illingworth explained the decision, but Gill was not convinced.
The India captain walked away shaking his head.
The delivery also appeared to be going over the stumps. So, even without an inside edge, the LBW decision would most likely have stayed not out. India lost their review.
Siraj, Jadeja miss out as India go in with four pacers; Pant returns
Gill won the toss and elected to bowl against New Zealand. 
Mohammed Siraj
 and Ravindra Jadeja were left out of the playing XI as India opted for a four-pronged pace attack.
Gill went with four pacers - Jasprit Bumrah, Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj and Prasidh Krishna. Washington Sundar was included as the spin-bowling all-rounder.
Rishabh Pant returned to the playing XI after recovering from injury, while Dhruv Jurel also made the cut as the second wicketkeeper-batter.

briefs.headline: Tom Latham equals Sehwag in unwanted batting record list after first over duck
briefs.deck: Latham's dismissal put him on an unwanted list of New Zealand captains. He became only the fourth Kiwi skipper to be dismissed for a duck in a home Test against India.
briefs.bodyText:
New Zealand captain 
Tom Latham
 was dismissed for a duck against India in the first Test of the two-match series at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Thursday, November 19. 
Jasprit Bumrah
 bowled the left-handed opener with the third ball of the match after India captain Shubman Gill won the toss and elected to field.
Latham's dismissal put him on an unwanted list of New Zealand captains. He became only the fourth Kiwi skipper to be dismissed for a duck in a home Test against India. Barry Sinclair was the first, while Stephen Fleming was the last to suffer the same fate before Latham. Fleming had scored a three-ball duck in the first innings of the January 1999 Test at Seddon Park in Hamilton.
The 34-year-old also equalled former India opener 
Virender Sehwag
 in the record for the most ducks by an opener in Test cricket. Latham has now been dismissed without scoring 15 times as an opener.
Most ducks as an opener in Test cricket
- 19 - Kraigg Brathwaite
- 17 - Mike Atherton
- 16 - Marvan Atapattu
- 15 - Virender Sehwag
- 15 - Tom Latham
Bumrah made an immediate impact on his return to international cricket, taking three wickets as India reduced New Zealand to 70/5 after lunch on the opening day. The 32-year-old pacer had been out of action for India since the second Test against South Africa in November last year, mainly because of injury.
New Zealand have been Bumrah's most difficult opponent in Test cricket in terms of his bowling average. While he has taken 52 Tests to build an overall average of 19.79, his nine wickets in five Tests against New Zealand have come at an average of 45.44.
Bumrah began his spell with the new ball after Gill elected to bowl on a green pitch. Bowling over the wicket, he pitched the ball around off stump to Latham, who chose to leave it, expecting it to move away. The delivery straightened and hit the top of off stump, giving India an early breakthrough.
Bumrah returned for a second spell before lunch and dismissed Daryl Mitchell. The batter had tried to counter the pacer by stepping down the pitch. Gill responded by placing a fielder close on the leg side, and the move paid off. Mitchell (1) edged the ball onto his pad before it carried to Yashasvi Jaiswal, who took the catch.
Bumrah struck again after lunch, having Tom Blundell caught by Gill at first slip. The wicket was his third of the innings. At the time of writing New Zealand were 117/5 in 43 overs.

briefs.headline: Magnus Carlsen sparks controversy, forfeits games against Bibisara on back-to-back days
briefs.deck: Magnus Carlsen was already out of the title race and was playing for a 17th-place finish. On Tuesday, he built an 11-point lead by winning three of the four blitz games and two rapid games against Bibisara. He took the same decision on Wednesday after collecting 10 points from the four blitz and two rapid games.
briefs.bodyText:
World No. 1 
Magnus Carlsen
 has landed in controversy at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot after forfeiting his Fast Classic games against Bibisara Assaubayeva on two consecutive days.
The Norwegian walked away from the playing hall after taking an unassailable lead in the tie. However, he did not inform his opponent, who was left waiting for him at the venue. Carlsen spoke to the arbiter before leaving.
Carlsen was already out of the title race and was playing for a 17th-place finish. On Tuesday, he built an 11-point lead by winning three of the four blitz games and two rapid games against Bibisara. He took the same decision on Wednesday after collecting 10 points from the four blitz and two rapid games.
Bibisara was awarded all eight points available on both days after Carlsen forfeited the classical games. Despite this, the Norwegian won the tie. He had taken the first day's fixture 11.5-8.5, while the second day ended in a 10-10 draw.
Magnus Carlsen explains why he forfeited the games
Carlsen defended his decision, saying there was no reason to play the classical game once the result of the tie had been decided.
"There will be no classical game as I understood, the match is over. 
The only consequence of not showing up is that you will lose a totally meaningless game," Carlsen was quoted as saying by Norwegian broadcaster TV2 on Tuesday.
"I think that if you play a World Championship and it counts for points and such, I can understand."
The decision also came at a difficult time for Carlsen's rating. A draw or defeat in the Fast Classic game would have taken him below the 2800 Elo mark for the first time in almost 17 years. He has stayed above the mark since 2009.
Carlsen has struggled in the Fast Classic format at the Budapest pilot. He finished fifth in his group after recording nine draws and one defeat in 10 games. His only loss came against Armenia's Haik Martirosyan.
The Norwegian also lost 21.8 rating points over the past week. He could now be at risk of losing the world No. 1 ranking, which he has held for more than 15 years.
Carlsen had also expressed his reluctance to play another classical game in the classification match earlier on Tuesday.
"This is an awkward situation to be in, I would rather not play that much more classical anymore," he said.
Total Chess to review format after Budapest pilot
Total Chess CEO Kjell Madland said the Budapest pilot would help organisers understand how the format works in actual competition. They will consider changes, if needed, before the first edition in March 2027.
"The Budapest pilot is an important learning exercise for Total Chess. While we have developed the format and regulations with considerable thought and input, the real test is how they work in a live competitive environment.
"We want to hear directly from the players and arbiters, understand their experiences and take on board constructive feedback.
"Our objective is to assess whether any refinements are required before the inaugural edition in March 2027. We are not approaching this with a predetermined view that the rules need to change; rather, we want to ensure that we have tested the format thoroughly and are taking the best possible version of it into its inaugural season," Madland said in a statement.
The organisers could not immediately confirm whether Carlsen would face an automatic fine for forfeiting the games.

briefs.headline: Gukesh asked to distance himself from 'what people are saying' ahead of World Championship
briefs.deck: Set against Cologny’s literary history, where Frankenstein and The Vampyre were conceived, the 2026 World Chess Championship pits reigning champion D Gukesh against Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov. Former challenger Peter Leko believes Gukesh must distance himself from expectations, as Sindarov now carries the favourite’s burden. He also welcomes the return of the demanding 14-game championship…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: In 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia unleashed one of the most violent volcanic eruptions in recorded history. Though its fury didn't stay buried in Indonesia. Ash and sulphur soon climbed into the atmosphere, altering weather patterns across the globe. Europe turned cold, wet and grey. The year 1816 would go down in history as the Year Without a Summer.
It was summer by the calendar, but nothing about it felt that way. A group of young English writers and intellectuals, Mary Godwin, who would later become Mary Shelley; her partner Percy Bysshe Shelley; the famous poet Lord Byron; his physician and fellow writer John Polidori; and Mary's stepsister Claire Clairmont, found themselves holidaying at Villa Diodati, Byron's rented residence overlooking Lake Geneva in Cologny, Switzerland.
Confined indoors by relentless rain and gloom, it was Byron who proposed they pass the dreary evenings with a ghost-story competition, each of them tasked with conjuring something frightening enough to unsettle the rest.
Initially, Mary struggled to find her idea, until a dream supposedly handed her one. It was a short story that would eventually swell into one of the most influential novels in the history of literature, Frankenstein.
Picture it for a moment. Some of the greatest literary minds of the Romantic era, trapped indoors by foul weather, daring each other to invent something terrifying.
That said, Frankenstein wasn't even the only invention born that night. Polidori's own short work of prose fiction, The Vampyre, emerged from the very same contest.
That one meeting in Cologny, 210 years ago, revolutionised literature by launching modern science fiction, reshaping Gothic horror, and creating the modern vampire archetype.
And now, in that same corner of Switzerland, something with the potential to leave a similarly lasting mark on the game of 64 squares is about to unravel. In a battle of 20-year-olds, India's Gukesh Dommaraju will take on Uzbekistan's Javokhir Sindarov for the World Chess Championship crown, in Geneva's Cologny, from November 24 to December 12.
The last time Switzerland hosted a World Championship was in 2004, when Vladimir Kramnik met Peter Leko in Brissago. It was a historic match in its own right, but that's a story for another day, because this time, Leko returns to Swiss soil not as a challenger but as a witness.
A lesson from the World Championship
"I learned a lot from that (2004 World Championship) experience. Going into a World Championship match, you have to distance yourself from all the expectations and from what people are saying," Leko, known to be one of the most respected voices in the world of chess, told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive conversation. Leko, who will share the official commentary duties with Russian Grandmaster Peter Svidler for the 2026 FIDE World Chess Championship, didn't need long to find a parallel from the reigning champion's own past.
"I would also like to relate this to Gukesh's match against Ding Liren," he said. "I felt that one of the reasons Gukesh lost the first game was the incredible hype surrounding him before the match."
It wasn't hard to see why that hype had built.
"He had a fantastic run, qualified for the Candidates, delivered a phenomenal performance at the Chess Olympiad, and his rating was booming. Ding Liren's rating was going down while Gukesh's was skyrocketing. Everybody was expecting Gukesh to crush Ding Liren," he recalled.
That weight of expectation, in Leko's reading, pushed Gukesh into a trap of his own making.
"I think Gukesh went into that first game feeling that he had to show the whole world that he was the hunter and that he wanted to dominate the match. It backfired with that terrible loss," the 47-year-old Grandmaster explained.
The rest, as chess fans will remember, turned into one of the most dramatic title matches in recent memory.
"That already signalled that it was going to be a hell of a match. And it certainly was a rollercoaster, which Gukesh eventually managed to win under dramatic circumstances."
Why the pressure has switched sides
If Gukesh walked into Singapore carrying the world's expectations, Leko believes he'll walk into Cologny carrying almost none of them; and that, this time, it's Sindarov who has to live with being the favourite.
"The expectations are now completely opposite," the Hungarian said. "Sindarov is the one who has had an incredible year, winning the World Cup in Goa, winning the Candidates, playing fantastic chess with the Uzbek team and winning the Chess Olympiad. He carries the expectations."
Gukesh, by contrast, gets to play the role he was denied last time.
"I believe that, from Gukesh's side, he doesn't care too much about the outside noise. He just wants to focus on himself and show the whole world, as well as himself, that he is capable of retaining his title and playing a fantastic match against Sindarov." Which, Leko says, sets up something close to a mirror image of the match he's already seen up close. "In this respect, I'm expecting a very close fight, just like the match between Ding and Gukesh two years ago."
Fourteen games much better for the match?
There's a structural significance to this match too, one that's easy to miss amid the psychological drama. When Kramnik met Leko in Brissago in 2004, it was a 14-game match. The cycles that followed shrank the format to 12 games, and it stayed that way for the best part of two decades until Magnus Carlsen's defence against Ian Nepomniachtchi in 2021 restored it to 14.
Gukesh and Sindarov will now play out that same 14-game format in Cologny. And Leko, unsurprisingly, is thrilled to see the longer format back.
"One other thing I'm extremely happy about is that the World Championship matches are back to 14 games, as they were last time. In between, we had those 12-game matches. I believe 14 games is much better for a World Championship match," the veteran Grandmaster, also coach of Germany's Vincent Keymer, opined.
"It means that the players are finally pushed to give absolutely everything they have. There is an enormous amount of preparation, tremendous tension and some crazy games. By the end, the players are completely exhausted.
"After all, this is about the title and becoming World Champion. You then have to play two additional games, the 13th and 14th. Those games are already extremely demanding because you're tired and exhausted, yet you still have to find incredible strength within yourself to keep delivering your absolute best in the final game."
A storyteller's seat in the 2026 World Chess Championship
Asked whether he's looking forward to commentating on the match, Leko's answer came without a beat of hesitation.
"Incredibly, I'm so happy. It's like a dream come true for me," he told this website. "I've already done commentary during World Championship matches, but only for a few games. With all my experience, I know exactly that a World Championship match is about so much more than moves and individual games. It's a whole story. Every small mosaic piece put together establishes the bigger picture of the match.
"As a commentator, together with Svidler, we'll have the opportunity, right from the beginning, to bring our audience into this magical world of the World Championship match. We'll be able to explain all the psychological moments, the expectations before the match and how everything surrounding the event has a huge impact. Then come the first game, every single move, the opening decisions, what we expect might happen and what makes sense from the players' teams' perspectives for the future.
"I think it will be a fantastic opportunity to go into real depth, not just commentate on the games and the moves, but tell the whole story. I'm really looking forward to a dramatic finish in this match."

briefs.headline: 19 straight Tests, same toss call: Shubman Gill continues Basin Reserve trend
briefs.deck: India's captain Shubman Gill won the toss and chose to bowl first against New Zealand in Wellington. The decision to bowl reflects a trend at the Basin Reserve, where teams have consistently preferred this option. Jasprit Bumrah made his comeback to the Test squad after a one-year hiatus. India aims to recover from a 3-0 Test series defeat against New Zealand in 2024.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India captain 
Shubman Gill
 won the toss and opted to bowl against New Zealand in the first Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Thursday. India have gone in with four fast bowlers, while 
Jasprit Bumrah
 returns to the Test team after a year.
The decision to bowl extended a remarkable trend at the Wellington venue.
Teams winning the toss have opted to bowl in 19 consecutive Tests at the Basin Reserve, including this match.
The last captain to choose batting after winning the toss at the venue was Daniel Vettori against Pakistan in 2011.
The pitch conditions could have influenced Gill's decision. The surface remained under covers due to rain over the past few days and overnight. When the covers were removed on Thursday morning, the pitch had a green appearance with a thin layer of grass.
However, the surface might not offer as much help to the fast bowlers as its appearance suggests. It could provide pace and bounce only after drying out and losing its initial moisture. The average first-innings score at the Basin Reserve is 313.
Bumrah returns as India go with four fast bowlers
Bumrah made his return to the Test side after a year. Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj and Prasidh Krishna are the other three fast bowlers in the playing XI. 
Washington Sundar has been selected as the spinning allrounder.
India have also included both wicketkeeper-batters 
Rishabh Pant
 and Dhruv Jurel, with Pant taking responsibility behind the stumps.
Mohammed Siraj and Gurnoor Brar have been left out, while Ravindra Jadeja has also missed out on selection.
Gill admitted that picking the bowling combination was a difficult decision.
"Quite tough, you know. We were contemplating for the past one week which combination to, you know, go with because all of our fast bowlers have been doing really well. You know, very difficult for Siraj and Gurnoor for both of them to miss out, you know. They did decently well in the ODI series. Siraj and Gurnoor obviously, you know, was man of the series there. So it was a hard decision for us. But hopefully, you know, all the fast bowlers that we picked, they should be able to do the job for us," Gill said.
Explaining the decision to bowl first, the India captain said: "Yeah, definitely we've seen there's a bit more initially in the wicket as compared to the second innings. So hopefully we are able to exploit that."
India look to bounce back against New Zealand
India will be keen to avenge their 3-0 Test series defeat at home against New Zealand in 2024.
Their recent record in New Zealand has also been disappointing. India have not won a Test in the country since 2009, when they registered their first series victory there in 41 years.
India failed to win a Test during their 2013 and 2019 tours. Their only victory at the Basin Reserve came during their maiden tour of New Zealand in 1968.

briefs.headline: Litton Das scripts history, Bangladesh keeper sets world record in South Africa Test
briefs.deck: Wasim Bari, Bob Taylor, Ian Smith, Ridley Jacobs and Joshua Da Silva had all recorded seven dismissals in a Test innings. Da Silva was the last to achieve the feat, in 2023.
briefs.bodyText:
Bangladesh wicketkeeper Litton Das created a new world record for the most dismissals by a wicketkeeper in a single Test innings, taking his tally to eight against South Africa in the ongoing first Test at the Wanderers in Johannesburg. He broke the record on the fourth morning when he stumped Kagiso Rabada, moving past the previous mark jointly held by five wicketkeepers.
Wasim Bari, Bob Taylor, Ian Smith, Ridley Jacobs and Joshua Da Silva had all recorded seven dismissals in a Test innings. Da Silva was the last to achieve the feat, in 2023.
Litton also became the first wicketkeeper to score a century and take eight dismissals in the same Test innings. Before him, Denis Lindsay in 1966 and 
AB de Villiers
 in 2013 had scored a hundred and taken six dismissals in an innings. Both had achieved the feat in Johannesburg.
Litton had taken six catches by the end of the third day, dismissing Aiden Markram, Zubayr Hamza, Michael Breetzke, Wiaan Mulder, Marco Jansen and Simon Harmer. He added the stumpings of Ryan Rickelton and Rabada on the fourth morning to complete his record.
Litton had also contributed with the bat in the first innings, scoring 120 off 179 balls, including 14 fours and a six. 
He shared a 206-run partnership for the sixth wicket with Towhid Hridoy as Bangladesh posted 400, their highest total against South Africa.
Last month, Litton had recorded nine dismissals in a Test against Afghanistan, besides scoring a century and a half-century. He became the first wicketkeeper to achieve that combination in a Test and was named Player of the Match.
The Bangladesh ODI and T20I captain is now at the top of the country's list of wicketkeepers with the most Test dismissals, having accounted for 154. Mushfiqur Rahim is second with 113.
South Africa take control as Rickelton, Rabada lead the way
Meanwhile, South Africa took control of the first Test after Ryan Rickelton's century and an all-round contribution from Kagiso Rabada helped them build a first-innings lead of 157 runs.
South Africa posted 557, with Rickelton scoring 102 and sharing a 117-run eighth-wicket partnership with Rabada, who made 72. Captain Temba Bavuma remained unbeaten on 68.
Bangladesh struggled in their second innings and ended Day 4 at 100-5. Their troubles began after lunch when Marco Jansen dismissed Tanzid Hasan for four.
Rabada then bowled Mominul Haque for one before Simon Harmer had Najmul Hossain Shanto caught at slip for 11. Harmer went on to bowl debutant opener Mahfijul Islam for 32, while Rabada removed first-innings centurion Towhid Hridoy, who was caught behind for 23.
Mushfiqur Rahim, on five, and Litton Das, on 12, were at the crease when bad light and rain brought an early end to the day's play.

The duo of Henry Nicholls and Glenn Phillips have been brillaint and their partnership is proving to be a crucial one in the context of the game. The Indian shoulders are starting to drop as they're unable to break through, but they have to keep digging in and be patient because the sun is baking the surface, making it a bit easier for batting.
Anshul Kamboj to Glenn Phillips, A well-directed bumper, banged in over middle and leg. Phillips gets inside the line and falls over a bit but manages to pull it down to fine leg for a single.
Anshul Kamboj to Henry Nicholls, That's sloppy from Akash Deep. Good length on middle and leg, Henry Nicholls just clips it to mid on, where Akash is lazy to get down and lets it through his hands. Nicholls ends up picking up three runs as Akash tracks back and throws it back in.
Anshul Kamboj to Glenn Phillips, Back of a length and over off, nudged down through the point region for a single by Phillips.
Anshul Kamboj to Glenn Phillips, A floaty delivery from Kamboj, full and outside off, shaping away. Phillips has a waft at it and goes for an expansive cover drive but is beaten past the outside edge.
Anshul Kamboj to Glenn Phillips, Hitting the deck hard, pulling the length back a bit and over off stump. Phillips pats it back down the track.
Anshul Kamboj to Henry Nicholls, Kamboj begins on a straighter line, drifting on the pads, and Nicholls clips it between square leg and mid-wicket for a single.
Anshul Kamboj replaces Akash Deep.
Washington Sundar to Glenn Phillips, Tossed up on off, not all that full. Phillips lunges ahead and blocks it to the right of the bowler.
Washington Sundar to Glenn Phillips, Back to over the wicket to the right-hander, drifting it down leg. Phillips stays back and nurdles it past leg slip.
Washington Sundar to Glenn Phillips, Full-ish length around off, darting it away from the batter. Phillips covers the line well and defends it off.
Washington Sundar to Henry Nicholls, Full and wide outside off, Henry Nicholls jams the cover drive into the turf and hits it toward extra cover for a quick single.
Washington Sundar to Glenn Phillips, Quicker and flatter, pushed across the right-hander. Phillips leans on, opens the bat face and pushes it through cover-point for a single.
Washington Sundar to Glenn Phillips, Floated up around leg stump, Phillips leans on, lifts one leg up and flicks it straight to mid-wicket.
Akash Deep to Henry Nicholls, Hard length now, in and around off stump. Nicholls covers the line well and keeps it downon the deck.
Akash Deep to Henry Nicholls, Good-length delivery, angled into middle and leg, Nicholls blocks it down the pitch.
Akash Deep to Glenn Phillips, On the shorter side again, over middle stump. Glenn Phillips hangs back and pulls it a bit uppishly through mid-wicket for a single. Also, Akash has overstepped again and a No Ball is called.
Akash Deep to Henry Nicholls, Top fielding from Devdutt Padikkal. Short-pitched delivery over middle, Henry Nicholls nails the pull down to the right of mid-wicket, where Padikkal lunges across and makes a fine half stop, keeping it down to a single.

briefs.headline: Testing times: On India’s two-Test series against New Zealand
briefs.deck: India needs to be at its best in Tests against New Zealand
briefs.bodyText:
New Zealand at home remains an indomitable cricketing opposition. Even the great West Indian squad led by Clive Lloyd suffered a 0-1 Test series defeat in 1980. Pitches that look lush as English meadows, the wind that is often bone-chilling cold, and fast bowlers relishing their prospects, make any tour of New Zealand a difficult outing. So far, the visiting Indians have done well, having won the T20I and ODI series, but the real contest starts with the first Test at Wellington’s Basin Reserve from Thursday. The Shubman Gill-led men’s last overseas tour of Sri Lanka ended with a middling 1-0 victory in the two Tests, but more needs to be done against New Zealand in the latest two-Test series. Placed fourth in the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) table, and with hopes of securing a final berth seemingly fragile, India is in a win-all-games situation first up against New Zealand and later when Australia arrives next year. Against current WTC topper New Zealand, the Indian batters have to stay anchored. This is a line-up that no longer has Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Cheteshwar Pujara and Ajinkya Rahane. Gill and company get another opportunity to reiterate their credentials.
For some rugged inspiration they need not look beyond coach Gautam Gambhir in their dressing room. The doughty former India opener batted for 643 minutes while scoring a match-saving 137 in the Napier Test during the 2009 tour. The southpaw will be hoping that the current batting unit, which is high on flair, will remain sober and effectively counter the host. K.L. Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Devdutt Padikkal and Gill have the onerous task of negating the New Zealand seamers in their backyard. Rishabh Pant and Dhruv Jurel add depth, and if the former can successfully unleash his maverick batting approach, India can upset the host’s best-laid plans. New Zealand will miss the retired Kane Williamson but its batters would be comfortable on familiar surfaces. For India, much would hinge on how Jasprit Bumrah bowls. If the spearhead clicks, then it becomes easier for much of his support-cast that includes the persevering Mohammed Siraj, who was a touch rusty in Sri Lanka. From the squads of the past to the present unit, Ravindra Jadeja remains the link. Whether he will get a role to play or whether the management prefers an all-pace attack, remains a matter of conjecture. The home team led by Tom Latham will depend on Matt Henry, Kyle Jameson and other pacers, to choke the Indian batters. A hard task awaits India, first at Wellington and then at Christchurch.
